How to Scale Mixture-of-Experts: From μ\muP tothe Maximally Scale-Stable Parameterization

Leena Chennuru Vankadara ††thanks: Equal first author. †Equal contributor. Correspondence to: l.vankadara@ucl.ac.uk. Equ This work does not relate to MH’s position at Amazon. Affiliation: Gatsby Computational Neuroscience Unit, University College London.    Moritz Haas. Affiliation: Amazon    Luke Hayward Affiliation: Gatsby Computational Neuroscience Unit, University College London.    Sebastian Bordt Affiliation: University of Tübingen, Tübingen AI Center    Alessandro Breccia. Affiliation: Gatsby Computational Neuroscience Unit, University College London.
Abstract

Recent frontier large language models predominantly rely on Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures. Despite empirical progress, there is still no principled understanding of how hyperparameters should scale with network width NN, expert width NeN_{e}, number of experts MM, sparsity KK, and depth LL to ensure both stability and optimal performance at scale. We take a principled step toward resolving this gap by analyzing three different scaling regimes: (I) co-scaling N≍NeN\asymp N_{e}, (II) co-scaling N≍M≍KN\asymp M\asymp K, and (III) full proportional scaling of N,Ne,MN,N_{e},M, and KK. For each regime, we develop a novel Dynamical Mean Field Theory (DMFT) description of the limiting training dynamics of MoEs that provides a formal foundation for our analysis. Within this framework, we derive the unique parameterization for SGD and Adam satisfying all maximal-update (μ\mu) desiderata. We then show that the resulting μ\muP prescription does not reliably induce monotonic improvement with scale or robust learning-rate transfer. We trace these pathologies to scale-dependent observables in the aggregation dynamics, which motivates a refined set of desiderata that we term maximal scale stability. Guided by this principle, we derive a Maximally Scale-Stable Parameterization (MSSP) for both SGD and Adam in all three scaling regimes, and characterize the corresponding limiting dynamics - qualitatively distinct from the μ\muP limit - through a separate DMFT analysis. Experiments verify that MSSP robustly recovers learning rate transfer and monotonic improvement with scale across regimes. Combined with existing depth-scaling theory, these results provide a complete scaling prescription for MoE architectures as a function of width, depth, expert width, and number of experts.

1 Introduction

Scaling the number of parameters consistently improves network quality (Kaplan et al., 2020; Hoffmann et al., 2022), yet the cost of architectural and hyperparameter tuning grows alongside it. At the frontier, where models exceed hundreds of billions of parameters (Brown et al., 2020; Guo et al., 2025), even a single training run makes iterative tuning infeasible. An influential line of work proposes to design parameterizations under which finite-size networks can be regarded as discretizations of a well-defined infinite-size limit (Yang and Hu, 2021; Bordelon and Pehlevan, 2022; Bordelon et al., 2024b) - specifically, parameterizations under which feature and prediction dynamics remain approximately invariant across scales and finite networks closely track the limiting object. Under such parameterizations, smaller models serve as faithful proxies for larger ones: optimal hyperparameters, such as learning rates, transfer across scales (Yang et al., 2022; Everett et al., 2024; Dey et al., 2025), and performance improves predictably with scale (Yang et al., 2022; Dey et al., 2025). The Maximal Update Parameterization (μ\muP) is the canonical instance for width (Yang et al., 2022), with analogous prescriptions developed for depth (Bordelon et al., 2024b; Bordelon et al., 2024a; Dey et al., 2025).

While scale-invariant parametrizations for dense models are well-developed, modern frontier large language models increasingly employ Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) layers (Jiang et al., 2024; Guo et al., 2025), which decouple parameter count from computational cost via sparse routing (Shazeer et al., 2017). In doing so, they introduce additional scaling axes that must be coordinated jointly with width NN and depth LL: the number of experts MM, the expert width NeN_{e}, and the routing sparsity K/MK/M. Recent engineering advances render scaling along all of these dimensions practically tractable (NVIDIA, 2026), and a growing body of evidence indicates that increasingly fine-grained experts outperform configurations comprising a few large experts (Clark et al., 2022; Krajewski et al., 2024; Dai et al., 2024). Yet, little is known about how to optimally scale fine-grained, sparse MoE architectures, which motivates the question that this paper addresses:

How should MoE architectures and training hyperparameters be scaled to yield scale-invariant, non-degenerate feature and prediction dynamics in various co-scaling regimes of M,N,Ne,M,N,N_{e}, and KK?

As we will see in this work, developing scaling theories for MoEs is substantially more involved than for dense networks. One cannot generally assume commutativity across axes (M,N,Ne,KM,N,N_{e},K); instead, joint limits governed by their relative rates must be analyzed. Deriving such limits is technically challenging since routing and aggregation in MoEs couple the dynamics of the router, the experts, and update statistics (Shazeer et al., 2017; Fedus et al., 2022). This leads to a combinatorial space of co-scaling regimes, each, as we demonstrate, exhibit qualitatively distinct behavior.

Main Contributions. We study three co-scaling regimes for MoEs: (Regime I) N≍Ne→∞N\asymp N_{e}\to\infty with M,KM,K fixed; (Regime II) N≍M≍K→∞N\asymp M\asymp K\to\infty with NeN_{e} fixed - the fine-grained / bottleneck regime increasingly favored in modern MoE designs; and (Regime III) joint scaling N≍Ne≍M≍K→∞N\asymp N_{e}\asymp M\asymp K\to\infty. Across these regimes, we make the following contributions:

  • •

    μ\muP for MoEs across regimes and optimizers. In each scaling regime, we derive the parameterizations that satisfy the μ\muP desiderata for SGD and Adam via signal propagation analyses which are formally justified by a novel Dynamical Mean Field Theory (DMFT) for each scaling regime.

  • •

    Scale-dependence of μ\muP in MoEs. Despite formally satisfying the μ\muP desiderata, we find that μ−\mu-parameterizations do not reliably deliver learning-rate transfer or monotonic improvement with scale in MoEs (Fig. 1, 5 and 6). We trace this to scale-dependence in the training dynamics.

  • •

    Maximally Scale-Stable Parameterization (MSSP). We propose maximal scale stability as a refined principle generalizing μ\muP desiderata, and derive the Maximally Scale-Stable Parameterization (MSSP) for SGD and Adam in each regime. The required corrections to μ\muP are structurally distinct across regimes: zero router initialization in Regime I, amplified expert-output initialization variance (1/Ne1/N_{e} to M/NeM/N_{e}) in Regime II, and shared expert weights at initialization in Regime III.

  • •

    DMFT under MSSP. We derive a self-consistent DMFT for the limiting training dynamics in each regime under MSSP, including a four-level conditional mean-field hierarchy in Regime III induced by the shared expert initialization, qualitatively distinct from the limiting dynamics under μ\muP.

  • •

    Empirical validation. We verify on MLP and Transformer MoEs that MSSP robustly recovers learning-rate transfer, and restores monotonic improvement with scale across all three regimes. We provide a complete scaling prescription for modern Transformer MoE architectures along width NN, depth LL, number of experts MM, expert width NeN_{e} and number of active experts KK.

Overall, this paper takes important steps towards stable, predictable and optimal MoE scaling that preserves reliable hyperparameter transfer and monotonic improvement with increasing network size.

Independent and concurrent work. Jiang et al. (2026) derive a signSGD parameterization under Regime III via DMFT and present Transformer MoE experiments showing approximate LR transfer along individual scaling axes. We derive μ\muP for SGD and Adam across Regimes I, II, and III using a signal propagation analysis complemented by a DMFT for each regime, and our experiments scale jointly along the axes each regime prescribes. In Regime III, our μ\muP for Adam coincides with theirs for signSGD up to ϵ\epsilon scaling and a larger router initialization. Crucially, we identify that in Regimes II and III, μ\muP does not reliably yield learning rate transfer or monotonic improvement with scale in MoEs and propose MSSP as a resolution. In Regime III, our DMFT for MSSP is qualitatively distinct: it exhibits a four-layer mean-field hierarchy (versus a three-layer hierarchy under μ\muP), and we additionally derive novel DMFT limits for Regimes I and II under MSSP. See Appendix D for extended discussion.

Experiment Setup. Our experiments cover both MLP and Transformer MoEs. We utilize MLP MoEs to isolate scaling degeneracies at a manageable scale; this allows for the exhaustive hyperparameter tuning that would be computationally prohibitive with Transformers, which we reserve for validating our foundational claims. Specifically, we perform MLP MoE experiments with a single MoE block without residual connection but nonlinearity applied to ht0h^{0}_{t}. We train single pass using 100 classes of TinyImageNet (Le et al., 2015) with batch size 5050. This amounts to 10001000 steps over 5000050000 images. For each scaling configuration, we separately tune a global initialization multiplier and a learning rate multiplier for each weight matrix. Due to interactions between these multipliers, we sweep all six multipliers jointly at small size N=128N=128, amounting to at least 56=15 6255^{6}=15\,625 runs for each combination of parameterization and scaling regime.

In our transformer MoE experiments, we train GPTs where dense layers are replaced with MoE layers (Muennighoff et al., 2024). We train with warmup and cosine learning rate decay on Dolma3 (Olmo et al., 2025) up to width 2048 or 2.5B parameters using AdamW (Loshchilov and Hutter, 2019). We use RMS pre-norm and qk-norm and an auxiliary loss with weight 0.01 for load balancing (Shazeer et al., 2017). Open source code to fully reproduce our experiments is publicly available. All details can be found in . Additional coordinate checks, learning rate sweeps and supporting evaluations are provided in , for example showing the importance of multiplier tuning () and of layerwise Adam ϵ\epsilon-scaling ().

3 Maximal Update Desiderata for MoEs and their Shortcomings

The maximal-update (μ\mu) desiderata have served as the fundamental guiding principle for deriving principled scaling rules such as μ\muP for dense networks that deliver stable and predictable training dynamics, monotonic improvement in performance with scale, and learning-rate transfer across model sizes (Yang and Hu, 2021; Bordelon et al., 2024b; Vyas et al., 2024; Dey et al., 2025). A natural starting point for MoE scaling is therefore to seek a parameterization that satisfies these desiderata in each of our scaling regimes. We now recapitulate the μ\mu-desiderata and then derive the unique layerwise initialization and learning-rate scaling rules satisfying them in each regime. We will then see that, despite satisfying the μ\mu-criteria by construction, μ\muP can induce degeneracies in MoEs, motivating the refined desiderata we propose in the next section.

Norm choice. For any vector, matrix or tensor TT, we measure average entry size with the RMS norm ‖T‖RMS:=(1|T|​∑i∈entriesTi2)1/2\|T\|_{\mathrm{RMS}}:=\Big(\tfrac{1}{|T|}\sum_{i\in\mathrm{entries}}T_{i}^{2}\Big)^{1/2}, and measure spectral properties of matrices WW using the operator norm when equipping input and output space with ∥⋅∥R​M​S\|\cdot\|_{RMS}: ‖W‖op:=supx≠0‖W​x‖RMS‖x‖RMS.\|W\|_{\mathrm{op}}:=\sup_{x\neq 0}\frac{\|Wx\|_{\mathrm{RMS}}}{\|x\|_{\mathrm{RMS}}}.

Recapitulating the Maximal Update Desiderata. The μ\mu-desiderata for non-degenerate training dynamics under model scaling are captured in the following three criteria (Yang and Littwin, 2023). Intuitively, they require that parameter updates induce Θ⁡(1)\Theta(1) feature updates that propagate forward through all linear layers without vanishing or diverging.

For Adam, faithfulness ensures ϵ\epsilon scales as the layerwise gradient RMS norm11 1 Under infinite precision, gradient scaling is equivalent to scaling ϵ\epsilon, that is Ψ⁡(c⋅g,ϵ)=Ψ⁡(g,c−1⋅ϵ)\Psi(c\cdot g;\epsilon)=\Psi(g;c^{-1}\cdot\epsilon) for all c>0c>0. Numerically, scaling gradients or Adam’s moments mt,vtm_{t},v_{t} is more stable than scaling ϵ\epsilon.. ϵ\epsilon acts as a crucial scale-dependent hyperparameter: values that are too large relative to gradients lead to suboptimal performance, while values that are too small are numerically unstable (Everett et al., 2024). For homogeneous optimizers such as SGD and signSGD, faithfulness imposes no additional constraint, since gradient rescalings can be absorbed into an effective learning-rate rescaling.

We derive the b​c​d​αbcd\alpha-parameterizations that satisfy Desiderata μ\mu-1 to μ\mu-3 in each of our three scaling regimes. The derivation proceeds by analyzing forward and backward signal propagation through the network (App. F). For SGD the scaling is formally justfied by the corresponding DMFT description of the limiting training dynamics (App. G–App. ). For Adam, the scalings are heuristically derived. For the reader’s convenience, App. E provides a self-contained walkthrough of all mechanisms that underlie the scaling behaviour of MoEs in all three regimes, accessible without having to read the full technical derivation.

Empirical degeneracies of μ\muP in MoEs. Having established the unique μ\mu-parameterization for each regime, we now examine whether it robustly delivers the scaling benefits expected in dense networks such as learning-rate transfer and monotonic improvement with increasing scale.

Regime I. Under μ\muP, training in Regime I broadly behaves as expected: loss improves monotonically with scale, and learning-rate transfer holds across scales (). One empirical anomaly stands out: propagating updates of the router typically vanish with scale (), even though our derivation predicts them to be Θ⁡(1)\Theta(1). We will return to this discrepancy in Section 4.

Regimes II and III. Interestingly, however, we find that μ\muP can fail empirically in Regimes II and III: (i) Effective and propagating updates do not remain Θ⁡(1)\Theta(1) at initialization, and can take many steps to drift toward their predicted asymptotic values (Figure 4). (ii) Performance often degrades with scale (Fig. 1 and 3 and , App.  and ) and (iii) Learning rates that are optimal at small scales do not remain optimal at larger scales (Fig. 5 and 6, App.  and ). In short, μ\muP does not reliably deliver the scaling benefits in MoEs that motivate it in dense networks.

HP tuning. These findings are robust to extensive layerwise HP tuning conducted at N=128N=128 and transferred to larger scales (). We resolve the underlying mechanisms in the next section.

Diagnosing the mechanism for failure in Regimes II and III. To understand these empirical failures under μ\muP, examine the aggregation over experts unique to MoEs. The post-aggregation activations htl+1h_{t}^{l+1} can be written as htl+htaggh^{l}_{t}+h^{\text{agg}}_{t}, where htaggh^{\text{agg}}_{t} admits the following decomposition:

htagg=1M​∑i=1Mϕil⋅(W0l,out,i​h0,il,in⏟init.+Δ​Wtl,out,i​ht,il,in⏟effective+W0l,out,i​Δ​ht,il,in⏟propagating).h^{\text{agg}}_{t}\;=\;\frac{1}{M}\sum_{i=1}^{M}\phi^{l}_{i}\cdot\bigg(\underbrace{W^{l,\text{out},i}_{0}\,h^{l,\text{in}}_{0,i}}_{\text{init.}}+\underbrace{\Delta W^{l,\text{out},i}_{t}\,h^{l,\text{in}}_{t,i}}_{\text{effective}}+\underbrace{W^{l,\text{out},i}_{0}\,\Delta h^{l,\text{in}}_{t,i}}_{\text{propagating}}\bigg). (Agg)

A single principle organizes the scaling properties of each of these quantities. The cross-expert average exhibits LLN-like behaviour and contributes at Θ⁡(1)\Theta(1) whenever the per-expert summands share a coherent direction across experts; when the per-expert summands have independent random directions, the corresponding aggregate exhibits Central Limit Theorem (CLT)-like behaviour which suppresses a factor of M\sqrt{M}. The underlying mechanism that produces or destroys this coherence varies across these aggregate terms and across regimes, so they can occupy distinct orders in NN, and the order of htl+1h^{l+1}_{t} at any finite scale is set by whichever sub-term dominates. We now provide intuition for how each of these aggregates behaves. We recommend non-technical readers to skip to ‘Empirical consequences’.

Init aggregate. Each per-expert summand ϕil⋅W0l,out,i​h0,il,in\phi^{l}_{i}\cdot W^{l,\text{out},i}_{0}\,h^{l,\text{in}}_{0,i} is a chain W0l,out,i​W0l,in,iW^{l,\text{out},i}_{0}\,W^{l,\text{in},i}_{0} of two independent Gaussian matrices acting on the shared input x0lx^{l}_{0}. By rotation invariance, the cross-expert dependence between summands is mediated by its scaled norm, ‖x0l‖2/M\|x^{l}_{0}\|^{2}/M, which as M→∞M\to\infty converges to a deterministic scalar. Since summands are asymptotically i.i.d., the init aggregate exhibits CLT-like behaviour and is Θ⁡(1/M)\Theta(1/\sqrt{M}) in both Regimes II and III.

Propagating aggregate. The propagating aggregate admits a further decomposition. At leading order, Δ​htl,in,i≈W0l,in,i​Δ​xtl+Δ​Wtl,in,i​xtl\Delta h^{l,\text{in},i}_{t}\approx W^{l,\text{in},i}_{0}\,\Delta x^{l}_{t}+\Delta W^{l,\text{in},i}_{t}\,x^{l}_{t}, splitting the propagating aggregate into two contributions: 1M​∑iϕil​W0l,out,i​W0l,in,i​Δ​xtl\frac{1}{M}\sum_{i}\phi^{l}_{i}\,W^{l,\text{out},i}_{0}\,W^{l,\text{in},i}_{0}\,\Delta x^{l}_{t} and 1M​∑iϕil​W0l,out,i​Δ​Wtl,in,i​xtl\frac{1}{M}\sum_{i}\phi^{l}_{i}\,W^{l,\text{out},i}_{0}\,\Delta W^{l,\text{in},i}_{t}\,x^{l}_{t}. The former is governed by the same CLT mechanism as the init aggregate, with one caveat: Δ​xtl\Delta x^{l}_{t} depends on each W0l,in,iW^{l,\text{in},i}_{0} through backpropagation. However, a single vector in ℝN\mathbb{R}^{N} cannot align nontrivially with M→∞M\to\infty independent random Gaussian chains simultaneously. The per-expert summands therefore remain approximately independent across experts, and the same CLT argument applies. This contribution is therefore also of order Θ⁡(1/M)\Theta(1/\sqrt{M}) in both Regimes II and III. The second contribution behaves differently in different scaling regimes. Substituting the rank-one gradient Δ​Wtl,in,i∝(W0l,out,i)⊤​δtl+1​(xtl)⊤\Delta W^{l,\text{in},i}_{t}\propto(W^{l,\text{out},i}_{0})^{\!\top}\delta^{l+1}_{t}(x^{l}_{t})^{\!\top} (where δtl+1=∇htl+1ℒ\delta^{l+1}_{t}=\nabla_{h_{t}^{l+1}}\mathcal{L} represents the backpropagated error signal from the subsequent layer) yields the form 1M​∑i=1Mϕil​Gi​u\frac{1}{M}\sum_{i=1}^{M}\phi^{l}_{i}\,G_{i}\,u, where Gi:=W0l,out,i​(W0l,out,i)⊤G_{i}:=W^{l,\text{out},i}_{0}(W^{l,\text{out},i}_{0})^{\!\top} and u∝δtl+1u\propto\delta^{l+1}_{t} is shared across experts.

  1. (a)

    Regime II. When NeN_{e} is held fixed, GiG_{i} has rank Ne=Θ⁡(1)N_{e}=\Theta(1) and after rescaling, it is the orthogonal projector onto a O⁡(1)O(1) dimensional subspace of ℝN\mathbb{R}^{N} that is Haar-distributed on the Grassmannian Gr⁡(Ne,N)\mathrm{Gr}(N_{e},N) (i.e., uniformly random among NeN_{e}-dimensional subspaces), and these subspaces are independent across experts. Therefore, the per-expert vectors {Gi​u}i=1M\{G_{i}u\}_{i=1}^{M} are approximately i.i.d. across experts with no coherent direction, and the cross-expert average exhibits (CLT-like behaviour). Both contributions to the propagating aggregate are therefore Θ⁡(1/M)\Theta(1/\sqrt{M}) under μ\muP.

  2. (b)

    Regime III. When Ne≍NN_{e}\asymp N, W0l,out,iW^{l,\text{out},i}_{0} is generically full rank and the empirical spectrum of Gi=W0l,out,i​(W0l,out,i)⊤G_{i}=W^{l,\text{out},i}_{0}(W^{l,\text{out},i}_{0})^{\top} concentrates around its mean (Marchenko and Pastur, 1967). Consequently Gi≈c​ING_{i}\approx c\,I_{N} for a deterministic scalar c=Θ⁡(1)c=\Theta(1), so Gi​u≈c​uG_{i}u\approx c\,u for every ii. The per-expert summands therefore share a coherent direction uu, and this contribution exhibits a Law of Large Numbers(LLN)-like behaviour at Θ⁡(1)\Theta(1) scale. Together with the Θ⁡(1/M)\Theta(1/\sqrt{M}) first contribution, the propagating aggregate contains a strictly subleading contribution and exhibits a milder version of the same CLT/LLN imbalance. Moreover, the init term in both regimes exhibits CLT behaviour so remains subleading.

Effective aggregate. Substituting the rank-one gradient Δ​Wtl,out,i∝δtl+1​(ht−1l,in,i)⊤\Delta W^{l,\text{out},i}_{t}\propto\delta^{l+1}_{t}\bigl(h^{l,\text{in},i}_{t-1}\bigr)^{\!\top} reveals that the summands of the effective aggregate share a coherent direction δtl+1\delta^{l+1}_{t}. The effective aggregate therefore exhibits LLN-like behaviour at Θ⁡(1)\Theta(1) along δtl+1\delta^{l+1}_{t} in both Regimes II and III.

Empirical consequences. In summary, htaggh^{\mathrm{agg}}_{t} is composed of unbalanced contributions: the init term is of order Θ⁡(1/M)\Theta(1/\sqrt{M}) in both regimes; the effective term is of order Θ⁡(1)\Theta(1) in both; the propagating term decomposes into a first contribution of Θ⁡(1/M)\Theta(1/\sqrt{M}) in both regimes, and a second contribution of Θ⁡(1/M)\Theta(1/\sqrt{M}) in Regime II but Θ⁡(1)\Theta(1) in Regime III. The training-induced update Δ​htagg\Delta h^{\mathrm{agg}}_{t}, formed from the effective and propagating terms, is therefore unbalanced in both regimes, with the imbalance more pronounced in Regime II. This is confirmed empirically in Regime II under μ\muP (Fig. 3): at finite scale Δ​htagg\Delta h^{\mathrm{agg}}_{t} is dominated by the scale-suppressed init and propagating terms. Feature learning is therefore vanishing early in training and takes many optimization steps to become Θ⁡(1)\Theta(1) and performance consequently degrades with increasing scale (Fig. 1 and 3).

4 A More Fundamental Desideratum Beyond Maximal Updates: Scaling MoEs Requires Maximal Scale Stability

In Section 3, we traced the failure modes of μ\muP to scale-dependent contributions arising in the training dynamics. This motivates a more general and fundamental desideratum, which we call maximal scale stability: every primitive interaction obtained by decomposing each weight as W=W0+Δ​WW=W_{0}+\Delta W and propagating this split through the network should have a Θ⁡(1)\Theta(1) impact on the forward and (appropriately normalized) backward dynamics. For most settings of interest, this reduces to a compact set of operational conditions; we instantiate the desideratum for MoEs as follows:

We refer to a parameterization that satisfies these conditions as the Maximally Scale-Stable Parameterization (MSSP). For linear layers with diverging input and output dimensions (fan-in ≍\asymp fan-out), forward and backward desiderata coincide by the symmetry of the Gaussian initialization. MSSP desiderata reduce to μ\mu-desiderata in dense architectures such as MLPs and Transformers. But in general, forward scale stability does not imply backward scale stability as we will see below.

MSSP for MoEs. We derive parameterizations that satisfy the above desiderata in each scaling regime. The derivation proceeds analogously by analysing forward and backward signal propagation through the network (App. F), and is formally justified by the corresponding DMFT description of the limiting training dynamics (App.  and App. ).

Regime II (N,M,K→∞,Ne∈Θ(1))(N,M,K\to\infty,N_{e}\in\Theta(1)). Under μ\muP in Regime II, gradients at every layer except hl,out,ih^{l,\textrm{out},i} have scale-dependent contributions. In addition, we saw in Sec. 3 that both the forward and backward aggregations receive scale-dependent contributions. MSSP rectifies all these imbalances with a single intervention: the initialization variance of the expert output is amplified from 𝟏/𝐍𝐞\mathbf{1/N_{e}} to 𝐌/𝐍𝐞\mathbf{M/N_{e}}. Although failure modes in μ\muP arise through structurally distinct mechanisms, this variance amplification simultaneously rebalances every forward and backward cross-expert sub-aggregate, every previously sub-leading contribution to per-expert gradients as well as to the gradient flowing through the router (cf. tables in App. F.3.2 for μ\muP versus App. F.3.4 for MSSP).

The only quantity that does not remain Θ⁡(1)\Theta(1) under MSSP is the per-expert propagating update W0l,out,i​htl,in,i=Θ⁡(M)W^{l,\text{out},i}_{0}\,h^{l,\text{in},i}_{t}=\Theta(\sqrt{M}), which is impossible to avoid. We argue that this divergence is benign since its impact on the training dynamics is Θ⁡(1)\Theta(1), and no training observable inherits this divergence. The dynamics admits a well-defined DMFT limit under MSSP (App. ). We empirically verify that all relevant terms remain scale-stable over time (Figure 4, App. ). Consequently, MSSP-Regime-II restores both monotonic performance improvement with scale and learning rate transfer from small to large scale for both SGD and Adam (Fig. 1, 5 and 6, App. ).

Regime III (N,Ne,M,K,→∞)(N,N_{e},M,K,\to\infty). When Ne≍NN_{e}\asymp N, amplifying the expert output initialization variance induces divergence in the backward pass. The viable fix in Regime III is instead structural: share the expert initialization, 𝐖𝟎𝐥,out,𝐢=𝐖𝟎𝐥,out\mathbf{W^{l,\text{out},i}_{0}=W^{l,\text{out}}_{0}} and 𝐖𝟎𝐥,in,𝐢=𝐖𝟎𝐥,in\mathbf{W^{l,\text{in},i}_{0}=W^{l,\text{in}}_{0}} for all ii and the allow the routing mechanism to diversify experts over time. Under this intervention, complete scale stability is restored (see theory App. F.4.5 and experiment App. ). Figure 1 shows that this intervention can have impactful practical consequences: performance of both SGD and Adam on TinyImageNet reliably improves with scale only under MSSP but not μ\muP, all relevant quantities remain Θ⁡(1)\Theta(1) through training (see App. ), and learning rate reliably transfers across scales (Fig. 5 and 6).

Hence, both regimes call for structurally distinct interventions: increased expert output initialization in Regime II, and shared initialization in Regime III. Neither solution transfers to the other regime. A more detailed but intuitive mechanism-by-mechanism account of how the MSSP prescription rectifies each μ\muP failure is provided in App. E.

Regime I (M,K∈Θ⁡(1))(M,K\in\Theta(1)). μ\muP satisfies our operational MSSP desiderata for MoEs in Regime I. However, splitting Δ​hl−1\Delta h^{l-1} into the contributions of the router-gradient and the expert-gradient pathways reveals that the former is correlated with Q0Q_{0} and contributes coherently at Θ⁡(1)\Theta(1), while the latter is weakly correlated with Q0Q_{0} and is CLT-suppressed at Θ⁡(1/N)\Theta(1/\sqrt{N}). To recover residual balance in the router’s propagating update Q0l​Δ​hl−1Q^{l}_{0}\Delta h^{l-1}, MSSP initializes the router to zero. The empirical impacts of this adjustment are marginal (Figure 1, App. ).

Scaling depth LL. In residual MoEs, including Transformer MoEs, depth composes naturally with our analysis: once the per-layer MoE block is parameterized according to MSSP, with Θ⁡(1/L)\Theta(1/L) scaling of the residual MoE blocks (Dey et al., 2025), the analysis of Bordelon et al. (2024a) extends with minimal modification to give a well-defined infinite-depth limit. Table 1 gives a complete scaling prescription for modern transformer MoE architectures as a function of width NN, depth LL, expert width NeN_{e}, and number of (active) experts K,MK,M.

5 Self-consistent DMFT for MoE training dynamics

For each regime, we derive self-consistent equations describing the limiting MoE training dynamics using a path-integral formulation based on the Martin–Siggia–Rose–De Dominicis–Janssen (MSRDJ) framework Martin et al. (1973); De Dominicis (1976); Janssen (1976). This framework underlies pioneering DMFT analyses of training dynamics in infinite-width and infinite-depth deep neural networks Bordelon and Pehlevan (2022); Bordelon et al. (2024b); Bordelon et al. (2024a). We derive DMFT limits for MoE architectures in each of the three scaling regimes, under both μ\muP and MSSP; each admits a well-defined scaling limit. In each regime, the limiting MoE dynamics under MSSP enjoy several analytical properties described below. The full set of DMFT equations is provided in App.G-. We defer the comparison to μ\muP limits to App. .

Regime I (M,K∈Θ⁡(1))(M,K\in\Theta(1)). The DMFT has a finite-expert mean-field factorization. Residual-stream neurons and their backward signals are i.i.d. draws from a global single-site distribution; within each expert, hidden-layer neurons are i.i.d. draws from an expert-local single-site distribution. Both distributions are characterized self-consistently by a finite set of macroscopic order parameters. Because the number of experts is finite, the expert index is not replaced by a population mean field: the experts and router variables remain explicitly represented. Averages over the global distribution define the global feature and gradient kernels; Together with router variables, these order parameters close the limiting dynamics. Under soft routing, the stochastic router field vanishes in this limit, inducing deterministic routing. Without an additional symmetry-breaking mechanism (Top-KK, routing noise, or random router biases), the router remains uniform and experts stay identical throughout training. This is empirically verified in .

Regime II. The simultaneous N,M,K≍n→∞N,M,K\asymp n\to\infty limit with Ne∈Θ⁡(1)N_{e}\in\Theta(1) reveals a finite expert width mean-field factorization in MSSP. Residual-stream neurons and their backward signals are i.i.d. draws from an effective global single-site distribution; experts together with their router variables are i.i.d. draws from an effective expert/router distribution. Both are self-consistently characterized by a finite set of order parameters. Since per-expert hidden width is fixed, the hidden layer of a typical expert is a finite-dimensional component of the expert/router process. Averages over the global distribution define the global feature and gradient kernels; averages over the expert/router distribution define the routed expert-level kernels. These order parameters close the limiting dynamics.

Regime III. The simultaneous N,Ne,M,K≍n→∞N,N_{e},M,K\asymp n\to\infty limit reveals a four-level, conditional, mean-field hierarchy in MSSP. Schematically,

𝒳glob∼Pglob​(⋅,𝒦),ℱsh∼Psh​(⋅,𝒦),\mathcal{X}_{\mathrm{glob}}\sim P_{\mathrm{glob}}(\cdot;\mathcal{K}),\qquad\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{sh}}\sim P_{\mathrm{sh}}(\cdot;\mathcal{K}),
ℰ∣ℱsh∼Pex/r(⋅∣ℱsh;𝒦),𝒰∣(ℱsh,ℰ)∼Ploc(⋅∣ℱsh,ℰ;𝒦),\mathcal{E}\mid\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{sh}}\sim P_{\mathrm{ex/r}}(\cdot\mid\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{sh}};\mathcal{K}),\qquad\mathcal{U}\mid(\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{sh}},\mathcal{E})\sim P_{\mathrm{loc}}(\cdot\mid\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{sh}},\mathcal{E};\mathcal{K}),

where 𝒳glob\mathcal{X}_{\mathrm{glob}} denotes the global single-site process, ℱsh\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{sh}} the shared expert-hidden single-site process, ℰ\mathcal{E} the expert/router single-site process, and 𝒰\mathcal{U} the within-expert hidden-neuron single-site process.

Global single-site process. Residual-stream coordinates and their backward signals are i.i.d. draws from an effective distribution characterized self-consistently by a finite set of order parameters; averages over this process define the global feature and gradient kernels.

Shared expert-hidden single-site process. Coordinates of expert-averaged hidden-layer fields, arising from expert-averaged hidden activations and gradients, are i.i.d. draws from an effective shared distribution. Averages define the shared expert-hidden kernels, which summarize the correlation structure of these fields induced by the shared initial expert weights.

Expert/router single-site process. Conditional on the shared expert-hidden fields, expert/router sites are i.i.d. draws from an effective expert/router distribution; averages define expert-level kernels.

Within-expert hidden-neuron single-site process. Conditional on the shared expert-hidden fields and the corresponding router state, neurons in the expert hidden layers are i.i.d. draws from an effective distribution; averages define the expert-local forward and backward kernels.

The four processes form a closed self-consistent system: kernels defined at each level enter as parameters of the single-site distributions at the others, and the limiting dynamics are determined by solving all four levels simultaneously.

6 Discussion and Future Work

Scaling laws and hyperparameter transfer have become the backbone of modern model development. Yet, for MoE architectures there remained a critical gap of how to scale the optimization hyperparameters jointly with MoE model dimensions M,N,Ne,K,LM,N,N_{e},K,L. The Maximally Scale-Stable Parameterization (MSSP) introduced here closes this gap. We believe generalizing the μ\mu-desiderata to maximally scale-stable desiderata provides a framework for scale-invariant dynamics across a broader set of architectures, optimizers, and scaling dimensions, with practical benefits including predictable performance gains and hyperparameter transfer.

MSSP enables the first principled compute-optimal comparison of the three co-scaling regimes. Earlier work on optimal expert granularity (Clark et al., 2022; Krajewski et al., 2024; Dai et al., 2024) was conducted under suboptimal model scaling and merits reevaluation. More fundamentally, why hyperparameters transfer under scale-invariant parameterizations, in MoEs, dense networks, or beyond, remains an open theoretical problem.

The DMFT limits are of independent interest, opening routes to studying finite-size corrections, expert specialization, and the role of routing. They also provide a framework for analyzing auxiliary load-balancing and zz-losses, which we verify empirically do not alter the scaling exponents but may shed light on router collapse through their interaction with the limiting dynamics.

Limitations.

In Regime II, MSSP causes the per-expert pre-aggregation W0l,out,i​htl,in,iW^{l,\text{out},i}_{0}\,h^{l,\text{in},i}_{t} to scale as Θ⁡(M)\Theta(\sqrt{M}). Though its dynamical impact remains Θ⁡(1)\Theta(1), at very large MM this may raise numerical-precision concerns, which a fused kernel computing the cross-expert aggregate without materializing the per-expert quantity could address. Our DMFT derivations are at the level of physical rigor; fully rigorous proofs remain open. Of practical interest would also be an analysis that captures increasing sparsity M/K→∞M/K\to\infty.

Part I Quick Reference

This part serves as a concise entrypoint to the appendix that enables the reader to orient themselves quickly and to navigate the subsequent parts in a structured way. Appendix A provides a roadmap and suggested reading paths depending on the reader’s background and interests.

For practitioners, Appendix B concisely provides our complete MSSP scaling prescription for modern transformer MoE architectures.

Appendix A Appendix Roadmap and Suggested Reading Paths

The remaining parts of this appendix are self-contained and can be summarized follows:

  • •

    Part II (Background and Extended Related Work) provides background on the established infinite width literature, in particular the most common a​b​cabc-parameterizations for standard dense networks, necessary to understand our corrected parameterizations for MoEs (Appendix C) and a detailed account of related work (Appendix D).

  • •

    Part III (Theory) provides three complementary levels of formalism: an intuitive scaling explanation (Appendix E), followed by a full forward and backward signal propagation analysis for deriving the μ\muP and MSSP hyperparameter scaling rules in each scaling regime (Appendix F) followed by a rigorous self-consistent DMFT for μ\muP and MSSP in each of the three scaling regimes (Appendices G to ). Note that Regimes II and III provide differing challenges that require their own resolutions, both in terms of scaling and analysis technique. Whenever the DMFT equations for a differing parameterization our routing mechanism follows from an analogous derivation, we omit the duplication and just provide the final set of self-consistent DMFT equations.

  • •

    Part IV (Experiments) contains the experimental setup for our MLP MoE and Transformer MoE experiments (), followed by extensive empirical evidence for our claims about learning rate transfer and scaling properties of μ\muP and MSSP for both SGD and Adam in all 3 scaling regimes (). We close with further empirical scaling insights that practitioners should be aware of in Sections  to .

If you only have 30 minutes: read (i) Appendix B for our complete Mixtral-style MSSP recipe, and (ii) Section E.8 for the regime-by-regime summary of how μ\muP breaks and how MSSP fixes it.

For conceptual understanding: We recommend familiarizing oneself with the background on width scaling (Appendix C), then reading Appendix E for a comprehensive introduction into the scaling arguments necessary for understanding the signal propagation pathologies of MoEs and how to fix them. These arguments will provide the reader with tools that are more broadly applicable to similar scaling derivations for other non-standard architectures and optimizers. We then recommend reading the complete MSSP recipe for modern MoEs (Appendix B), and ending with a quick pass over the empirical results in . In particular, we recommend skipping Appendices F to during this first read.

Deep dive: For the ambitious reader, we recommend starting with the above path for generating sufficient conceptual understanding, before diving into the detailed signal propagation analyses in Appendix F, and the DMFT analyses in Appendices G to . The signal propagation analysis decomposes all terms in the training dynamics and determines their scaling with arguments from random matrix theory. This makes the order of contributions of all observables explicit. The DMFT provides complementary value by clarifying how different variables interact via evolution of their kernels.

Practitioners: For readers that are primarily interested in the practical takeaways, we recommend starting with our complete Mixtral-style MSSP recipe in Appendix B. Our Transformer setup is introduced in and our empirical findings are provided in .

Notation mapping. The notation in the appendix differs slightly from the main paper. For readability, we write out the theory for a single block, but, as is common in the related DMFT and μ\muP literature (Yang et al., 2022; Jiang et al., 2026), every derivation follows in the same way for the architecture that stacks multiple blocks that is considered in the main paper. A detailed explanation is provided in Section E.10.

Appendix B Complete Maximally Scale-Stable Parameterization for Mixtral-Style MoEs

Part II Background and Extended Related Work

This part collects background on existing width-scaling parameterizations and a detailed account of related-work.

Appendix C Background on Width-scaling Parameterizations

Table C.1 gives an overview over the most common a​b​cabc-parameterizations for training dense networks with SGD. Yang and Hu (2021) use width-dependent weight multipliers n−a⋅Wn^{-a}\cdot W to scale gradients and avoid layerwise learning rates. This extra degree of freedom introduces an equivalence class of valid μ\muP a​b​cabc-parameterizations. Mean field parameterization (Mei et al., 2018; Chizat and Bach, 2018; Bordelon and Pehlevan, 2022) is equivalent to μ\muP, using the multipliers fan-in-1/2 except N−1N^{-1} in the output layer. For practical readability, we remove this extra degree of freedom in the main paper by using naive weight multipliers a=0a=0 for all trainable weights.

μ\muP for Adam in standard architectures. Adam requires the same layerwise initialization variances as SGD. For clarity, consider the weight-multiplier-free version of μ\muP. Since Adam normalizes its update, but the update direction remains correlated with the incoming activations, Adam’s layerwise learning rate scaling simplifies to η​(W)=1/fan-in​(W)\eta(W)=1/\texttt{fan-in}(W) for any linear weight matrix W:ℝfan-in→ℝfan-outW:\mathbb{R}^{\texttt{fan-in}}\to\mathbb{R}^{\texttt{fan-out}}. For faithfulness, Adam ε⁡(W)\varepsilon(W) should always scale as the gradient RMS norm of WW, that is Θ⁡(1)\Theta(1) for the readout layer and Θ⁡(N−1)\Theta(N^{-1}) otherwise.

Baseline Parameterizations: SP and the μ\muP heuristic. Standard parametrization (SP) uses Xavier/Glorot-type variance scaling (Glorot and Bengio, 2010; He et al., 2015), i.e. typical dense layers take bW=12b_{W}=\tfrac{1}{2} (with common exceptions for input embeddings), and uses the same optimizer hyperparameters such as learning rate and Adam ε\varepsilon for all layers.

In contrast, μ\muP is designed so that maximal-update behavior (and, for adaptive methods, faithfulness) hold in the infinite-width limit for dense networks (Yang and Hu, 2021; Yang and Littwin, 2023). Practitioners often use the following μ\muP heuristic: classify a weight tensor by whether it maps fixed→n\to n (input-like), n→nn\to n (matrix-like), or n→n\tofixed (output-like), and assign (b,c,d)(b,c,d) accordingly as summarized in Table C.2. For MoEs in Regime I, this heuristic treats expert MLP weights matrix-like, while router projections are output-like due to the fixed number of experts MM. In Regime I, μ\muP heuristic indeed satisfies all μ\mu desiderata, but it does not suffice in Regimes II and III, when co-scaling the number of experts M→∞M\to\infty.

Appendix D Detailed Related Work

Mixture of Experts models. Mixture of experts models have a long history in machine learning (Jacobs et al., 1991), with instantiations such as hierarchical models (Jordan and Jacobs, 1994), Gaussian processes (Tresp, 2000) or Dirichlet processes (Shahbaba and Neal, 2009). After the first application in deep networks by Eigen et al. (2013), Shazeer et al. (2017) sparked the use of MoEs in modern architectures, using the top-kk operation for sparsification and trainable noise for load balancing. Fedus et al. (2022) lowered communication and computational cost for improved scalability, using Kaiming initialization and simplifying the load balancing auxiliary loss. Most MoE architectures still use a width-independent initialization of 0.0060.006 (Dai et al., 2024). The trend in recent frontier models goes toward increased fine-graining, from 2 out of 8 in Mixtral 8x7B and 8x22B (Jiang et al., 2024) to 8 out of 256 in Deepseek-R1 (Guo et al., 2025). Zoph et al. (2022) introduce the router z-loss for router logit regularization; Haas et al. (2025) suggest that miss-scaling causes logit divergence, hence the additional regularization might be unnecessary in MSSP. Insightful empirical investigations can be found in the fully open OlMoE report (Muennighoff et al., 2024). They identify removing the need for the load balancing loss as an important future direction, since it significantly constrains the model flexibility and may prevent experts from sufficiently specializing over the course of training. To date, the theory of MoEs is very limited. Chen et al. (2022) show that MoEs are able to learn data with cluster structure using two-layer nonlinear convolutional neural networks as experts.

Scaling theory. Infinite-width theory dates back to Neal (1996); Matthews et al. (2018); Jacot et al. (2018). The Tensor Program series (Yang, 2019; Yang and Hu, 2021; Yang and Littwin, 2023) has served as a crucial tool for developing flexible and general infinite-width theory allowing to study non-vanishing feature learning limits (Everett et al., 2024; Vankadara et al., 2024; Haas et al., 2025). This theory gave rise to the maximal update parameterization (μ\muP) (Yang et al., 2022) under which the optimal learning rate and further dynamical properties (Noci et al., 2024b) have been observed to transfer to larger model width. The mean-field parameterization is equivalent to μ\muP. DMFT has proven useful as it allows to simulate from the limit (Chizat and Bach, 2018; Mei et al., 2018; Bordelon and Pehlevan, 2022; Bordelon et al., 2024a). Similar techniques allow infinite depth limits (Bordelon et al., 2024b; Hayou and Yang, 2023; Noci et al., 2024a; Chaintron et al., 2026). These works apply depth-dependent scaling factors like L−1/2L^{-1/2} or L−1L^{-1} (Dey et al., 2025) to the residual stream; it remains open whether these interventions suffice. Dey et al. (2025) show that L−1L^{-1} outperforms L−1/2L^{-1/2} in Transformer training, but Sun et al. (2025) argue that scaling should depend on the layer index.

Scaling mixture of experts models. Clark et al. (2022); Krajewski et al. (2024) and Dai et al. (2024, Figure 3) all suggest that increasingly fine-grained experts outperform fewer larger ones in terms of learning performance, with saturating gains. Boix-Adsera and Rigollet (2025) prove an exponentially improved expressivity due to fine graining. Mayaki (2026) provides theory showing that performance can improve either by scaling active capacity or by increasing the number of experts, depending on the dominant bottleneck. In practice, eventually the increased communication cost of routing dominates compute-optimality considerations, but increasingly efficient implementations are being developed. NVIDIA (2026) provides a highly optimized distributed training framework across scaling regimes, that also allows efficient training with many fine-grained experts. He (2024) proposes PEER layers that take fine graining to the extreme. However, all existing works use suboptimal model scaling, hence it will be crucial to evaluate the impact of granularity on scaling in MSSP.

Independent and concurrent work. Jiang et al. (2026) derive a parameterization for Sign SGD in Regime III via a DMFT analysis, and present Transformer MoE experiments showing approximate learning rate transfer when scaling one axis at a time with all others fixed. We derive μ\muP for SGD and Adam across all three Regimes I, II, and III using a signal propagation analysis complemented by a DMFT for each regime, and our experiments scale jointly along the axes each regime prescribes. Our μ\muP in Regime III coincides with theirs up to a larger router initialization. More importantly, we identify that in Regimes II and III, μ\muP principles do not suffice to robustly yield learning rate transfer or monotonic improvement with scale in MoEs, due to scale-dependent dynamics, and we propose MSSP as a resolution. In Regime III, our DMFT for MSSP is qualitatively distinct: it exhibits a four-layer mean-field hierarchy (versus a three-layer hierarchy under μ\muP), and we additionally derive novel DMFT limits for Regimes I and II under MSSP. We provide a detailed account of further related work in Appendix D.

Under Regimes II and III (M,K→∞M,K\to\infty), μ\muP differs from shape-based μ\muP-heuristic. For dense networks, it is common to scale the layerwise initialization variance and learning rate of a weight matrix purely based on its shape (Yang et al., 2022; Yang et al., 2023), distinguishing input-like (fixed →∞\to\infty), hidden-like (∞→∞\infty\to\infty) and output-like (∞→\infty\to fixed) layers. Małaśnicki et al. (2025) apply this heuristic to MoEs, treating the router output-like in Regime I (M,K∈Θ⁡(1)M,K\in\Theta(1)). Table 1 shows that μ\muP-heuristic coincides with μ\muP in Regime I, but fails to induce all μ\mu-desiderata in Regimes II and III.

Part III Theory

Intuitive Scaling Explanation

This part of the appendix presents our scaling analysis at three levels of formalism, each progressively more precise. We start with an intuitive explanation in Appendix E, then provide the detailed signal propagation analysis in Appendix F, and finally provide a full DMFT analysis for each scaling regime in Appendices G, , , and .

Appendix E Intuitive Explanations of the Shortcomings of μ\muP for MoEs and How MSSP Fixes Them

To set the stage for our formal results, we provide intuition for how to derive scaling rules for MoE blocks that satisfy Desiderata 1 and 2. In each scaling regime, these desiderata determine a unique (b,c,d,α)(b,c,d,\alpha)-parameterization (up to the rescaling invariance of homogeneous optimizers discussed in Section 2). Table 1 reports a canonical parameterization of this equivalence class. The SGD scaling in each regime is formally justified by the corresponding DMFT derivation. In addition, Adam scaling is heuristically derived but is directly guided by the same DMFT analysis. The conditions under which these parameterizations satisfy Desideratum 3 are discussed in Section F. Here and throughout, asymptotic notation (e.g., Θ⁡(⋅)\Theta(\cdot)) is understood with respect to the joint scaling trajectory 𝒮⁡(n)\mathcal{S}(n) as n→∞n\to\infty, specialized to the scaling regime (I–III) under consideration. For the intuitive explanation, we focus mainly on Regimes II and III. Regime I is more straightforward and is omitted for brevity.

E.1 Overview

Let’s start by recalling the Maximal update desiderata22 2 We omit an explicit discussion of the optimizer faithfulness desideratum here for brevity but we will briefly discuss ϵ\epsilon scaling..

E.1.1 Maximal Update Desiderata

The Maximal Update Desiderata require that in each layer, the effective and propagating updates remain Θ⁡(1)\Theta(1) in RMS at some t>0t>0:

‖𝒯effℓ​(t)‖RMS=‖Δ​Wtℓ​xtℓ−1‖RMS=Θ⁡(1),‖𝒯propℓ​(t)‖RMS=‖W0ℓ​Δ​xtℓ−1‖RMS=Θ⁡(1).\|\mathcal{T}^{\ell}_{\mathrm{eff}}(t)\|_{\mathrm{RMS}}=\|\Delta W^{\ell}_{t}\,x^{\ell-1}_{t}\|_{\mathrm{RMS}}=\Theta(1),\qquad\|\mathcal{T}^{\ell}_{\mathrm{prop}}(t)\|_{\mathrm{RMS}}=\|W^{\ell}_{0}\,\Delta x^{\ell-1}_{t}\|_{\mathrm{RMS}}=\Theta(1). (E.1)

For the MoE aggregation layer, we additionally require that the updates to the aggregated representation remains non-vanishing and non-diverging:

‖Δ​htagg​(t)‖RMS=Θ⁡(1).\|\Delta h^{\mathrm{agg}}_{t}(t)\|_{\mathrm{RMS}}=\Theta(1). (E.2)
E.1.2 Effective and propagating updates

Alignment exponents for effective and propagating updates. In all regimes, the asymptotic scales of forward and backward effective and propagating terms are governed by the training-induced correlation structure between the two factors appearing in each product. Following Yang et al. (2023); Everett et al. (2024), we summarise this effect via alignment exponents pℓp_{\ell} and qℓq_{\ell} (pℓ∇p^{\nabla}_{\ell} and qℓ∇q^{\nabla}_{\ell} analogously for backward), defined by

‖Δ​Wtℓ​xtℓ−1‖RMS\displaystyle\|\Delta W^{\ell}_{t}x^{\ell-1}_{t}\|_{\mathrm{RMS}} =Θ⁡((ninℓ)pℓ​‖Δ​Wtℓ‖RMS​‖xtℓ−1‖RMS),\displaystyle=\Theta\!\left((n_{\mathrm{in}}^{\ell})^{p_{\ell}}\,\|\Delta W^{\ell}_{t}\|_{\mathrm{RMS}}\;\|x^{\ell-1}_{t}\|_{\mathrm{RMS}}\right), (E.3)
‖W0ℓ​Δ​xtℓ−1‖RMS\displaystyle\|W^{\ell}_{0}\Delta x^{\ell-1}_{t}\|_{\mathrm{RMS}} =Θ⁡((ninℓ)qℓ​‖W0ℓ‖RMS​‖Δ​xtℓ−1‖RMS),\displaystyle=\Theta\!\left((n_{\mathrm{in}}^{\ell})^{q_{\ell}}\,\|W^{\ell}_{0}\|_{\mathrm{RMS}}\;\|\Delta x^{\ell-1}_{t}\|_{\mathrm{RMS}}\right),

where ninℓ:=dim(xℓ−1)n_{\mathrm{in}}^{\ell}:=\dim(x^{\ell-1}) denotes the fan-in of layer ℓ\ell. Informally, pℓp_{\ell} quantifies the degree of alignment between Δ​Wtℓ\Delta W^{\ell}_{t} and the current features xtℓ−1x^{\ell-1}_{t}, while qℓq_{\ell} quantifies the degree of alignment between the initial weights W0ℓW^{\ell}_{0} and the upstream feature change Δ​xtℓ−1\Delta x^{\ell-1}_{t}.

From (pℓ,qℓ)(p_{\ell},q_{\ell}) to scaling rules for optimizers. Fix a layer ℓ\ell and suppose the alignment exponents (pℓ,qℓ)(p_{\ell},q_{\ell}) are known. Assume inductively that at some time t>0t>0 the previous-layer quantities satisfy ‖xtℓ−1‖RMS=Θ⁡(1)\|x^{\ell-1}_{t}\|_{\mathrm{RMS}}=\Theta(1) and ‖Δ​xtℓ−1‖RMS=Θ⁡(1)\|\Delta x^{\ell-1}_{t}\|_{\mathrm{RMS}}=\Theta(1).
